segments.text: 1. The Nest. Zero Minutes.
This afternoon, somebody at The Nest has emptied a whole wallet onto the shared table and laid every note in a straight line.
The oldest and most crumpled at one end and the crispest at the other, with a single cowrie shell at the head of the row like a chairman.
And beside it, a yellow sticky note carrying one word in capital letters. Switzerland.
Whose wallet it is, I will tell you before we close.
Chale, how the thing be go?
I am Kofi, the editor.
This is the Gold Coast Pallava and this fourth edition costs about 50MB.
The thing be say we all know they hold.
The one price on this paper is something the Sedi cannot change.
If you have not watched our first two editions, go back for them first
because the gold Asante owed Britain in the first
and the gold scheme I promised to put a price on in the second, both come back today to collect their bill.
2. Front Page. 050.
Page 1. And, as the house rule goes, every headline is a question.
Our lead.
How did a little seashell, carried here from islands in the Indian Ocean, give its name to the money in your pocket?
Is the CD really printed in Switzerland, as your uncle swears at every funeral?
How did Ghana create billions of CDs in 2022 without switching on a single printing press?
Why, from December, will Kwame Nkrumah be the only one of the big six left on our money?
And, tucked in the corner like a classified ad,
which empire's money did Ghana throw away for decimals almost six years before that empire did the same thing at home?
3. Lead Story, 125.
Do you remember the gold of our first edition?
In Quy, gold and money share one word, Sika.
Because for centuries on this land, money was gold dust,
weighed on small brass scales against little cast figures we now call gold weights.
And the smallest weight in that system was the Pesawa.
So the coin in your pocket is, by its very name, a pinch of gold.
But gold was for big deals.
And for buying fish, there were cowries, the small white shells the Akan called sidye.
And they did not come from our beaches.
Most were gathered in the Maldives, islands in the Indian Ocean,
and carried to West Africa in the holds of European ships,
often as ballast, in a trade that also bought human beings.
Then, in the second half of the 1800s, merchants shipped in so many cheaper shells from East Africa
that the Kauri lost most of its value along the West African coast.
And that, my people, is the first inflation in this story.
Too many shells chasing too few goods.
The British replaced shells with shillings.
From 1912, a West African currency board, sitting in London, issued one currency for Nigeria,
the Gold Coast, Sierra Leone, and the Gambia, backed by reserves held in London.
So the colony's money was only as free as London allowed.
On the 14th of July, 1958, 16 months after independence,
the New Bank of Ghana issued the Ghana Pound.
Our own notes at last.
But still, pounds, shillings, and pence,
until Nkrumah decided that a free country should count in tens.
4. The Wire, 2.45
On Monday, the 19th of July, 1965,
in the cool, grey middle of the rainy season,
when Accra wakes under low cloud and the open gutters still hold the night's rain,
Ghanaians queued at bank counters with pound notes in their hands to meet a new money,
the Sidi, named after the Sede, the Kaori, and divided into 100 Pesues, the old gold weight.
One Sidi was worth 8 shillings and 4 pence.
One Ghana Pound bought two Sidi's and 40 Pesues,
and on the front of every note was one face, the President's, Kwame Nkrumah's.
In the silent film of those cues, people hold the new notes up to the light,
as if checking whether freedom had a watermark.
Four days after the Sedi was born, in Washington,
President Lyndon Johnson signed a law taking the silver out of America's dimes and quarters,
because the silver had become worth more than the coins it was stamped into.
Two countries in one week, both admitting that money is a promise, not a metal.
Nkrumah's Sidi lived 19 months.
After the coup of February 1966, the soldiers of the National Liberation Council issued a new Sidi on the 17th of February 1967.
One new Sidi for one Sidi and 20 Pesues, with Nkrumah's face removed.
On the 9th of March 1979, another military government changed the notes again,
and kept 30% of the cash you brought to the counter, and half of anything above 5,000 Sidi's.
And by 2007, the biggest note, 20,000 Sidi's, was worth about $2.
So on the 1st of July 2007, four Sidi's were cut off, and 10,000 old Sidi's became one Ghana Sidi.
5. The Palava Desk, 413.
Now the Palava your uncle started.
Is the Sidi printed in Switzerland?
Here is the record.
The Bank of Ghana does not print its notes at home.
It buys them from a tiny club of security printers, fewer than 20 in the whole world by the count of its currency head, Dominic Owusu.
For years, the main printer was Delarue in Britain, and a former deputy governor, Emmanuel Asiedumante, said Ghana had also used firms in Germany and France.

The 100 and 200 Sidi notes of 2019, and the 5 Sidi note for our 60th anniversary, were printed by an American company, Crane Currency, which beat five rivals, among them, yes, a Swiss one, Aurel Fusli of Zurich.
For the new notes launched this month, the bank has not publicly named the printer.
So there is no public record of the Sidi being printed in Switzerland.

The nearest Switzerland comes is the ink, because one Swiss company, Sikpa, near Lausanne, supplies the security inks on most of the world's banknotes, though whether that includes ours is not public.
But Chale, that question is staring at the wrong machine.
Most Sidi's are never printed at all.
Ghanaians moved 4.54 trillion Sidi's on mobile money in 2025 alone, and new money is created whenever the Bank of Ghana lends.
In 2022, it lent the government, through an overdraft, about 7% of everything the economy produced, created with keystrokes.
That year, the Sidi lost about 30% against the dollar.
Inflation reached 54.1% in December, so 100 Sidi's bought what 65 had bought a year earlier.
And on the 19th of December, Ghana stopped paying most of its foreign debts.
If you asked, how much have you been planting, that year, and flinched, you had met monetary policy.
Monetary policy, plainly, is the Bank of Ghana setting the price of money.
Its policy rate is what banks pay to borrow from it.
Raise it, and loans cost more.
Spending slows, and prices calm down.
Cut it, and money gets cheaper.
After 2022, that rate climbed to 30%.
The IMF lent $3 billion under a program Ghana completed on 27th of July this year.
Inflation fell to 5.5% in October.
And on the 18th of November, the bank cut its rate from 14% to 11%.
And the bill I promised you in our second edition.
The IMF says the bank's gold purchase program lost more than $1.7 billion in 2025,
while also crediting it with strengthening the reserves.
The Bank of Ghana and Goldbod have defended the program and disputed how its losses were described.
We print both, and you weigh them.
6. Then vs. Now
Then, in 1965, there was one face on every note.
Now, on Thursday, the 12th of November, 2026,
at Bank Square in Accra,
President Mahama launched the Heritage Series.
Eight notes, eight faces.
Agnes Tago Kwakupome,
remembered as the first Makola trader to open a bank account on the one city.
Cardinal Peter Porekuderi, on the two.
Kweji Agri, on the five.
Justice Annie Jaggi, on the ten.
The composer Ephraim Amu,
the second of the two men our Amu, the discerning, is named after, on the twenty.
Theodosia Oko, who designed our flag, on the fifty.
Kofi Annan, on the hundred.
And on the two hundred,
the face the soldiers removed in 1967,
now the only one of the big six left on our money,
Kwame Nkrumah.
The notes stay on cotton, not plastic, because of our heat.
They are smaller,
they carry features to help people with sight loss tell them apart,
and from the first of December,
they circulate beside the old notes,
which stay legal tender.
The palava came within a day.
Theodosia Oko's nephew said the face on the fifty looked more like her sister,
Dr. Letitia Obeng.
The bank replied on the 13th
that the portrait was built from photographs of Theodosia Oko herself,
and the minority in parliament wants to know what the whole exercise cost.
And the money in your own pocket?
It has never been easier to move money,
and it is no easier to keep its value.
A three-month treasury bill now pays about four and a half percent a year,
while prices rise by about five and a half,
so money that sits still is quietly shrinking.
And here is the item in the corner of page one.
Ghana dropped pounds, shillings, and pence for the decimal sedi in July 1965,
and Britain itself did not go decimal until the 15th of February 1971,
so the colony counted in tens almost six years before the empire did.
You know be small thing.
7. The team aside.
Back at the nest, the wallet on the shared table belongs to Kwame, the combative,
who arrived this morning with a bet.
His uncle had told him the CD is printed in Switzerland,
so he emptied his wallet and held every note up to the window,
looking for the words,
Made in Switzerland,
and found a watermark, a security thread,
and no country at all.
When Baba, the ascendant,
slid the crane currency story across to him,
he clung to the ink,
and I let him keep half a point.
Then I told him the Bank of Ghana begs us not to crumple,
staple, or spray our notes at parties,
and the combative,
who had planned a money bouquet for a friend's birthday,
went quiet,
smoothed every note flat with the side of his hand,
and put them back in his wallet one by one,
the oldest last.
I will tell you more about Kwame in good time.
8. The Editor's Note
9 o'clock
When I read Psychology,
the lesson that stayed with me
was that a promise is only as strong
as the number of people who believe it,
and a banknote is exactly that,
a promise printed on cotton.
Britain or America can print the paper,
only we can print the belief,
and every government that spends faster than it earns
is spending that belief.
9. The Letters Page
Letters Page
And this week's question asks for a lesson.
When prices rise faster than your savings earn,
what is one thing you, your family,
or your susu group does to stop your money from shrinking?
Tell us in the comments and I will pin the most useful answer.
10. The Dispatch
That is the fourth edition of the Gold Coast Pallava.
Complete, checked, stamped,
priced at about 50MB,
filed and signed at the Nest
266 Sandpiper Loop
or Nipa Enclave
and dispatched to Accra,
to Kumasi,
to Bunkpurugu,
to Half Asni
and to the world.
Squad,
better time.
